General.Description:
Harriet Voss was a successful environmental lawyer living in Edinburgh when she applied for a residency program that offered selected participants the use of a remote mountain bothy in the Scottish Highlands for one year, with no obligations, no Internet access, and no neighbours within twelve kilometres.

She expected to write a book. She expected to think more clearly. She expected the silence. She did not expect how loud the silence would turn out to be, or what it would say once she started listening.

Wild Hours is the memoir of that year — the practical realities of living alone without modern convenience (the firewood, the water supply, the long winter evenings), and the interior experience of being forced, finally, to spend sustained time in one's own company. Voss is a precise and honest writer who does not romanticise solitude — she describes anxiety, loneliness, and boredom with the same clarity she brings to the first snowfall, the red deer in the meadow at dusk, the particular satisfaction of a fire that catches first time.

She did write the book. Not the book she expected. This one.

Rare and true.
